name: Purchasing Power Parity
aliases: The purchasing-power-parity theory of exchange rates
statement: Exchange rates should adjust until the same basket of goods costs the same across countries.
statementAccent: the same basket of goods costs the same
meaning: Purchasing power parity holds that exchange rates should move so that an identical basket of goods costs the same in every country once prices are converted into a common currency. It extends the law of one price, which says a single good with no trade costs should sell for the same everywhere, from individual goods to whole national price levels. In its absolute form the exchange rate equals the ratio of the two countries' price levels; in its weaker relative form the rate of change of the exchange rate matches the difference in their inflation rates.
mechanism: The underlying force is arbitrage in tradable goods: if a basket were cheaper in one country, trade and the shifting of demand toward the cheaper location would push prices and the exchange rate toward equality. Absolute parity fixes the level of the exchange rate by the ratio of price levels, so that a given sum buys the same real basket anywhere. Relative parity is more forgiving, requiring only that a country with higher inflation see its currency depreciate at a matching rate. Because much of an economy is not traded across borders, the force acts strongly on tradables and only weakly on the whole basket.

examples.text: If a basket costs a thousand dollars in New York and six thousand Hong Kong dollars in Hong Kong, absolute parity implies an exchange rate of six Hong Kong dollars per US dollar.

GDP measured at purchasing power parity corrects for differing price levels, giving a truer comparison of output and living standards than market exchange rates, which is why a country's income can look far larger on a parity basis.
The Economist's Big Mac index is a light implementation of parity whose basket is a single good, a McDonald's burger, used to gauge whether currencies are over- or under-valued.

variants.name: Absolute versus relative parity
variants.text: Absolute parity equates the exchange rate to the ratio of price levels; relative parity, a weaker claim, equates the change in the exchange rate to the inflation differential between the two countries.

variants.name: The Balassa-Samuelson effect
variants.text: The systematic tendency for price levels to be higher in richer countries, because higher productivity in their traded-goods sectors raises the prices of non-tradables, producing a predictable departure from parity.

whyItMatters: It is foundational to international economics and exchange-rate theory, and it is the standard basis for meaningful comparison of output and living standards across countries, since parity-adjusted GDP corrects for the price-level differences that market exchange rates ignore. It gives a benchmark for judging whether a currency is over- or under-valued and a long-run anchor for thinking about where exchange rates should settle, shaping how economists compare economies and how bodies like the World Bank report global income.

working.text: use purchasing-power-parity rates, not market rates, when comparing real output or living standards across countries.

working.lead: Treat it as a long-run anchor
working.text: expect parity to hold only as a slow tendency, not at any given moment, since market rates deviate widely and persistently.
apply the logic most strongly to traded goods and least to services and other non-tradables, which are not linked internationally.

limits: Parity does not hold in the short or medium run; deviations are large and persistent. The market exchange rate is more volatile than the parity rate because it responds to shifting demand for currencies. Non-tradable goods and services are not linked across borders, transport costs and trade barriers weaken the law of one price, and countries consume different baskets, all of which drive departures. The Balassa-Samuelson effect makes price levels systematically higher in richer countries, and the persistence of deviations, with half-lives of several years, is the well-known purchasing-power-parity puzzle. It works as a long-run tendency, better for tradables than for the whole economy.
misreadings: Parity does not hold at every moment, and market exchange rates do not continuously equal parity rates; deviations are substantial and long-lasting, which is why the market rate and the parity rate routinely diverge. The Big Mac index is not a precise measurement but a deliberately light, single-good illustration. And parity is not equally valid for the whole economy: it bites on tradable goods and holds far more weakly for services and other things not traded across borders.
origin: Named and developed by the Swedish economist Gustav Cassel, who introduced the phrase in his 1918 paper 'Abnormal Deviations in International Exchanges' and elaborated it in post-war memoranda for the League of Nations, building on the law of one price and a lineage of ideas traced to the sixteenth-century School of Salamanca.
